paras: The attempted lynching of Shack Johnson took place in Winchester, Virginia, early on August 28, 1903, when a crowd beat Johnson, a Black man accused of assaulting councilman and night watchman James M. Haymaker, and tried to shoot him at the police station. An officer snatched the revolver away and Johnson was locked in a cell; less than a month later he was indicted, tried and sentenced to nine and a half years in the penitentiary within a few hours. White papers in Virginia, Washington and West Virginia treated it chiefly as an attack on a prominent citizen in which the accused "narrowly escaped lynching."

Haymaker, "one of the most prominent citizens of Winchester" in the Richmond Times-Dispatch's words, was a Confederate veteran, councilman and night watchman for Baker & Co., wholesale grocers. Late on Thursday, August 27, Johnson and a second Black man quarreled, by one account over some women in an alley, by another while cursing along the railroad track. When Haymaker ordered them to stop, Johnson reportedly knocked him down and the two kicked him unconscious; the Times-Dispatch said he was also beaten with his own revolver. Charles Brown, described as "a colored man," was credited with scaring the attackers off.

A search followed, and Johnson was found several hours later. According to the Martinsburg Herald, he "resisted arrest" and was beaten almost senseless by "the infuriated crowd," which twice stopped him on the way to the station house "with the intention of lynching." At the station a member of the mob pressed a revolver against his breast, and an officer snatched the weapon away. The Alexandria Gazette reported that his scalp was laid open "in numerous places by members of the mob who sought to kill him." The Times-Dispatch's correspondent said only that police kept "an infuriated crowd of armed men" from attempting a lynching and hurried Johnson into a steel cage.

The hunt for the second man went on: on Monday night, August 31, searching parties of young men who heard he was at the house of Mollie Smith, a Black woman, broke down her door and fired revolvers inside. Several "well-known white men" were arrested on Smith's complaint and were discharged in the Winchester Police Court. On September 5 Police Chief S. A. Seabright and two officers led armed men after the fugitive, by then named Thomas, to a Clarke County cornfield, where he escaped.

A special grand jury indicted Johnson, a special term was called at once, and he was tried, convicted and sentenced to nine and a half years the same day. Harry Thomas was indicted at the same time, and after his capture in Pennsylvania he was sentenced on February 18, 1904, to seven years. No report of charges against the men who beat and threatened Johnson appears in the coverage.

The first reports appeared on August 29: a short wire item in the Washington Times and a longer version of the same text in the Alexandria Gazette under "EXCITEMENT IN WINCHESTER." The Times-Dispatch's own front-page special, "Drunken Negroes Attack Captain J. M. Haymaker," called the accused "two drunken negro brutes" and gave the would-be lynchers one sentence crediting the police; the Clarke Courier reprinted it on September 2. The most detailed account of the crowd's violence came a week later in the Martinsburg Herald, headlined "NARROWLY ESCAPED LYNCHING" over "NEGROES MAKE A BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WATCHMAN."

The house raid drew sharper labels: the Alexandria Gazette headed it "WOULD-BE LYNCHERS," while calling Johnson "an negro tough," and the Martinsburg Herald reprinted it as "MOB AT WINCHESTER" with the subhead "Hot headed Young Men Create a Serious Disturbance." The one-day trial was reported under the headlines "QUICK TRIAL" and "Speedy Justice," with no mention of the mob, and no Black-press report of any part of the case was found.

The second accused man was first named Harry Wilshire or Wiltshire, Henry Thompson, or Harry Johnson before later reports settled on Harry Thomas. Early reports of his arrest, one of a "Wiltshire" jailed in Maryland, conflict with the September manhunt and his 1904 capture in Pennsylvania. The 1904 report gave Johnson's sentence as "ten years" rather than the nine and a half in the trial reports.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Shack Johnson
bases: A crowd beat Shack Johnson during and after his capture and tried to shoot him at the police station, but officers kept him alive and jailed him (A2, A3, A7); the attempt to kill is coded in the lynching elements.

The Times-Dispatch's own Winchester special (A3) and the separate wire carried by the Alexandria Gazette and Martinsburg Herald (A2, A7) agree that an armed crowd tried to lynch Johnson after his capture and that police stopped it.

accounts.gist: The police prevented 'an infuriated crowd of armed men' from attempting to lynch Johnson, who was hurried to jail and put in a steel cage; no beating is mentioned.

accounts.label: Martinsburg Herald account
accounts.gist: Johnson 'resisted arrest' and was beaten almost senseless by the crowd, was stopped twice on the way to the station by men intending to lynch him, and had a revolver held to his heart at the station door until police took it.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'Drunken Negroes Attack Captain J. M. Haymaker', called the accused 'drunken negro brutes' and reported the would-be lynchers in one sentence crediting the police.

The Martinsburg Herald's 'NARROWLY ESCAPED LYNCHING / NEGROES MAKE A BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WATCHMAN' gave the crowd's violence in detail without comment, and its 'MOB AT WINCHESTER' item called the raiders 'Hot headed Young Men'.
The Alexandria Gazette labeled the house raiders 'WOULD-BE LYNCHERS' while calling Johnson 'an negro tough'.
The same-day indictment, trial and sentence ran as 'QUICK TRIAL' and 'Speedy Justice'.

info: Assault on Haymaker late Thursday night, Aug. 27, 1903 (about 10-11 p.m. or 'midnight'); Johnson captured 'several hours later' and attacked by the crowd on the way to and at the station, i.e. early Aug. 28.
Winchester, Va.; the crowd's attack took place on the way to and at the police station house.
Shack Johnson, described as a 'negro', beaten and threatened with a revolver by the crowd.
Accused, with a second man, of knocking down, kicking and beating Capt. James M. Haymaker, councilman and night watchman, after Haymaker ordered them to stop cursing.
Unnamed: 'an infuriated mob' (A2), 'an infuriated crowd of armed men' (A3), 'the infuriated crowd' (A7); no member identified and race not stated.
Johnson sentenced to nine years six months in the penitentiary (A11-A13; 'ten years' in A15). Harry Thomas, caught in Pennsylvania, sentenced to seven years on Feb. 18, 1904.
